371.quote_or_event: “The second–lābha antarāya–hinders him from attaining any gain even though he sets his heart on it. … The fifth–vīrya antarāya–prevents effort or exertion, although he wants to make an effort or exert himself.”
371.explanation: Jain karma theory has an 'obstructive' karma (antarāya), one subtype of which blocks gain and another blocks energy or exertion. When it ripens, a person can want to strive and still find the effort will not come. In Jainism this karma is subtle matter the soul itself has bound, not a decree from outside.
371.tie_back: Valluvar says the fate of gain shows itself as tireless effort and the fate of loss as idleness. Pūjyapāda likewise explains failures of both gain and exertion by karma working within the person's own capacities.
371.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.13, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
371._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Strong fit on fate or karma working through effort and slackness. However, Jainism treats karma as self-made and removable, and Mahāvīra openly rejected the Ājīvika doctrine that all things are fixed (the Saddālaputta episode), so 'uzh' should not be read as fatalism here.

372.quote_or_event: “Gñânâvaranîya (which acts as an obstruction to right knowledge)” … “Obstruction of knowledge is fivefold (viz. obstruction to): a. Sruta, knowledge derived from the sacred books; b. Âbhinibôdhika, perception; c. Avadhigñâna, supernatural knowledge; d. Manahparyâya, knowledge of the thoughts of other people; e. Kêvala, the highest, unlimited knowledge.”
372.explanation: The first of the eight karmas is knowledge-obscuring karma. It clouds every level of understanding, from book learning up to omniscience, so that how clear or dull a person's mind is depends partly on how much of this karma is active.
372.tie_back: Valluvar says a fate of loss makes even a clever person foolish while a fate of gain widens understanding. Jainism likewise explains the dulling and widening of intellect by the rise or loosening of a particular karma.
372.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.2 and 33.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
372._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; diacritics simplified from the site's markup. A reasonable but partial fit. The text lists the karma and does not tie it to gain or loss of wealth as the kural does, and Jainism traces it to the soul's own past acts rather than to fate.

373.quote_or_event: “The dispassionate man who has performed all duties will quickly remove the obstructions to right knowledge and to right faith, and whatever Karman produces obstruction (to righteousness). Then he knows and sees all things, he is free from delusion and hindrances.”
373.explanation: In Jainism, perfect knowledge (kevala jñāna) is the soul's own nature. It is not built up from study but revealed once the obstructing karmas are removed, and book learning (śruta) is only one limited, partly covered form of it.
373.tie_back: Valluvar says that however many subtle books one studies, the knowledge that is truly one's own prevails in the end. The Jain idea of an innate knowledge, uncovered rather than acquired, offers a parallel to that 'true knowledge' (unmai arivu).
373.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.108–109 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
373._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. This is an interpretive bridge, so it is scored below 60. The kural credits one's native understanding to fate, while the Jain text describes the soul's innate omniscience being uncovered by dispassion. The resemblance is real but not one-to-one.

374.quote_or_event: “Antarâya is fivefold as preventing: 1. gifts; 2. profit; 3. momentary enjoyment; 4. continuous enjoyment; and 5. power.”
374.explanation: Jainism keeps the karma that blocks profit and enjoyment (antarāya) separate from the karma that obscures knowledge (jñānāvaraṇīya, 33.4). Because they are distinct karmas, a person's share of wealth and share of wisdom are governed separately.
374.tie_back: Valluvar observes that fate works in two different ways, one making people rich and the other making them wise. The Jain list of karmas likewise assigns gain and understanding to two different karmic causes.
374.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.15 (cf. 33.2–4) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
374._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A strong structural parallel: separate karmas for gain and for knowledge explain why wealth and wisdom do not come together. The text only implies the kural's point that the rich are often not wise; it does not say it.

375.quote_or_event: “The Karman in question brings about an obstruction to the enjoyment, &c., though all other circumstances be favourable.”
375.explanation: Explaining the obstructive karma, Jacobi, following the commentators, notes that it blocks enjoyment and gain even when every outward condition is right. Karma can override good circumstances.
375.tie_back: Valluvar says that in getting wealth, fate can turn every favourable circumstance against a person. The Jain gloss makes the same point: obstructive karma defeats gain 'though all other circumstances be favourable'.
375.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 33.15, Jacobi's footnote (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
375._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Note that this is Jacobi's explanatory footnote, based on the commentators, not the sūtra text itself. It matches the first half of the kural; the reverse case, bad circumstances turned good, is not stated.

376.quote_or_event: “Time elapses and quickly pass the days; the pleasures of men are not permanent; they come to a man and leave him just as a bird leaves a tree void of fruit.”
376.explanation: King Brahmadatta, enjoying the rewards of past merit, admits to the monk Citra that worldly pleasures cannot be held: they settle on a person and then leave, like birds deserting a tree once its fruit is gone. Citra had already told him that every deed bears its fruit (13.10).
376.tie_back: Valluvar says what is not one's allotted share will not stay however carefully guarded. The Jain image of pleasures leaving a man as birds leave a fruitless tree expresses the same idea: when the karmic fruit is spent, possessions go.
376.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.31 (cf. 13.10) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
376._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: the verse matches the first half (what is not one's own does not stay). The second half, that one's own share cannot be thrown away, is only implied by Citra's teaching that deeds inevitably bear fruit.

377.quote_or_event: “The third–bhoga antarāya–hinders the enjoyment of consumable things, though he is desirous of enjoyment. The fourth–upabhoga antarāya–prevents the enjoyment of non-consumable things, although he is eager after enjoyment of such things.”
377.explanation: Jainism separates owning things from being able to enjoy them. Two subtypes of obstructive karma block the enjoyment of consumables and of lasting goods, even when the person has them and wants to enjoy them.
377.tie_back: Valluvar says even those who amass crores can enjoy only as much as has been apportioned to them. The Jain account of enjoyment-obstructing karma makes the same distinction between possessing and enjoying.
377.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.13, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
377._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one on possession without enjoyment. Where commentators read Valluvar's 'Apportioner' (vakuththaan) as God, Jainism disagrees: there is no ordainer, and the apportioning is done by the soul's own karma.

378.quote_or_event: “By pondering (on what he has learned) he loosens the firm hold which the seven kinds of Karman, except the Âyushka (have upon the soul); he shortens their duration when it was to be a long one; he mitigates their power when it was intense.” … “By austerities he cuts off the Karman.”
378.explanation: Jainism agrees that bound karma has to come to fruition, but holds that reflection and austerity (tapas) can shorten it, weaken it, and wear it away before it ripens in full. That process, nirjarā, is the purpose of renunciation.
378.tie_back: Valluvar suggests the destitute would renounce if destined suffering did not still have to be lived through. Jainism accepts that karma must be dealt with but answers differently: renunciation and austerity are how destined suffering is cut short.
378.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.22 and 29.27 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
378._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Partial fit that partly contrasts with the kural. Both agree karma cannot simply be skipped, but Jainism holds it can be shed by austerity, which shifts the kural's pessimistic emphasis.

379.quote_or_event: “By conquering his passions he becomes free from passions; thereby he becomes indifferent to happiness and pains.”
379.explanation: In Mahāvīra's lecture on exertion in righteousness, conquering the passions (kaṣāya) brings an evenness in which pleasure and pain, both seen as the ripening of karma, no longer cause elation or distress.
379.tie_back: Valluvar asks why those who welcome good fortune should grieve at misfortune, since both come from the same source. The Jain ideal of being indifferent to happiness and pain gives that even-mindedness a practical basis.
379.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.36 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
379._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong thematic fit on equanimity toward good and bad fortune. The Jain verse grounds it in conquering the passions rather than in the kural's argument that both come from the same fate.

380.quote_or_event: “Every good deed will bear its fruit to men; there is no escape from the effect of one's actions.”
380.explanation: The monk Citra tells King Brahmadatta that both of their present lives, one a monk and the other a king, are the unavoidable results of earlier deeds. In Jainism the force no plan can outrun is the ripening of one's own karma, not an external fate.
380.tie_back: Valluvar ends the Book of Virtue by asking what is mightier than fate, which gets there first whatever way of escape one plans. The Jain answer is that 'there is no escape from the effect of one's actions'.
380.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
380._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Reasonable but partial: both see the force as inescapable, but Jainism rejects fate as an independent power. Mahāvīra argued against the Ājīvika view that 'all things are unalterably fixed' (Saddālaputta episode of the Uvāsagadasāo, read in a jainworld.com retelling), and he held that karma can be destroyed by austerity.
